claims.text: Severe plastic deformation can produce an ultrafine-grained microstructure in stainless steel.
Ultrafine-grained stainless steels produced by severe plastic deformation generally have better corrosion resistance than coarse-grained stainless steels.
Grain refinement increases the density of grain boundaries.
The increased grain-boundary density provides fast diffusion pathways for chromium.
Severe plastic deformation accelerates chromium migration from the stainless-steel bulk to the surface.
Ultrafine-grained stainless steel forms a chromium-enriched passive film.
Chromium enrichment of passive films on ultrafine-grained stainless steel has been observed using XPS and scanning-transmission electron microscopy.
The passive film on severe-plastic-deformation-processed stainless steel forms more quickly than on coarse-grained steel.
The passive film on severe-plastic-deformation-processed stainless steel is thicker than that on coarse-grained steel.
Greater chromium enrichment of the passive film is responsible for improved corrosion resistance in ultrafine-grained stainless steel.
Severe-plastic-deformation-processed stainless steel will have a lower corrosion rate than a coarse-grained control under identical conditions.
The reduction in corrosion rate will be statistically significant.
The proposed effect applies when stainless steel contains sufficient chromium and passivation governs corrosion resistance.
The proposed effect may fail at extreme temperatures or under non-oxidizing conditions where other corrosion mechanisms dominate.
The proposed corrosion-resistance mechanism is relevant to both chloride-rich aqueous solutions and operational molten salts.
The magnitude of corrosion improvement and the long-term stability of the ultrafine-grained structure remain undetermined.
